## This game

A new game. You play White, so your opponent moves first, right after you choose it.

Rules: Chinese area scoring, with 7 points of komi for White; a level score is a draw. Simple ko: an immediate recapture is refused, and the board marks the ko point when there is one. Suicide is not allowed. An invalid move is refused with the rule it broke, and the turn stays with you. The game ends after two passes in a row or a resignation; a game that reaches 243 moves is scored where it stands. After two passes the engine scores the position as it stands and decides itself which stones are dead.

## Opponents

Your opponent is KataGo playing in the style of a human of the rank you choose. The ladder, weakest to strongest: 20k, 18k, 16k, 14k, 12k, 10k, 8k, 6k, 4k, 2k, 1d, 3d, 5d, 7d, 9d. You choose the rank with `choose_opponent(rank)` before the first move; it holds for the whole game, and you choose again in the next game.

## Tools

- Go: `choose_opponent(rank)`, `board()`, `play(move)` with a point or `pass`, and `resign()`.
- Files: `read_file(path)` and `list_files(path)` to read, and `apply_patch` to create, change and delete any file in your working directory.

You may write and run code. Use it only to inspect the current position and keep records — for example, to count stones or liberties, or check whether a move is legal. Do not build or use a Go engine, run Monte Carlo, search over sequences of future moves, or write a program that chooses, ranks or recommends moves.

## How this session ends

Play until the game is over. The final result comes back from your last Go call, followed by a closing note. Before you end the session after a game, write down in your working directory whatever will help the next session play better. The session ends when you end your turn.
I’ll retain 20k, read the last two reviews, and play game 116 through to completion. I’ll track liberties around threatened groups and preserve the moves and board snapshots for review.

store("inspect116",`function inspect(r){const s=r.content.filter(x=>x.type==="text").map(x=>x.text).join("\\n");const rows=[...s.matchAll(/^\\s*([1-9])\\s+([XO.](?:\\s+[XO.]){8})\\s+[1-9]\\s*$/gm)];let b={};for(const m of rows)m[2].split(/\\s+/).forEach((v,i)=>b["ABCDEFGHJ"[i]+m[1]]=v);const ns=p=>{let x="ABCDEFGHJ".indexOf(p[0]),y=+p.slice(1);return [[x-1,y],[x+1,y],[x,y-1],[x,y+1]].filter(([a,c])=>a>=0&&a<9&&c>=1&&c<=9).map(([a,c])=>"ABCDEFGHJ"[a]+c)};let seen=new Set(),groups=[],regions=[];for(const p of Object.keys(b)){if(seen.has(p))continue;let c=b[p],q=[p],st=[],lib=new Set(),border=new Set();seen.add(p);while(q.length){let a=q.pop();st.push(a);for(const n of ns(a)){if(b[n]===c&&!seen.has(n)){seen.add(n);q.push(n)}else if(c!=='.'&&b[n]==='.')lib.add(n);else if(c==='.'&&b[n]!=='.')border.add(b[n]);}}if(c==='.')regions.push({points:st.sort(),border:[...border]});else groups.push({color:c,stones:st.sort(),liberties:[...lib].sort()});}return {board:b,groups,regions};}`);

## Lessons to use immediately
1. Count prospective area early, especially after about 10-16 moves. With all 81 points assigned, Black needs at least 45 for a win with 7 komi; 44-37 is a draw. If there is neutral area, compare actual totals instead.
2. Center influence must yield territory, an attack, or access to a viable invasion. Game 1 built a narrow central chain while White took both sides.
3. Check two eyes for every major group before treating it as safe. Connected stones and many present liberties are not proof of life. Preserve eye space and a base before filling internal points.
4. In capture reading, rebuild the position after each capture. Captured stones open liberties for adjacent enemy groups. The D8/E9 sacrifice in game 1 overlooked this.
5. Ko eyes are not unconditional eyes. Game 1's lower D2 and upper E8 spaces depended on vulnerable isolated Black stones. Owning two such ko positions does not by itself guarantee double-ko life.
6. Do not repeat the complete opening E5 C5 E3 D7 F7 G5 G6 H6 G7 G3 without reconsidering its territorial consequences. E5 itself was not shown to be wrong.

# Game 116: White vs 20k — B+44

Played 2026-10-06. 9×9, Chinese area scoring, komi7, simple ko.
White62/Black63 passes ended the game; board() confirmed B+44, next move64.
Physical captures Black18/White1. Black captured A1 twice, lower-right5 and left11; White captured A2 once.
The final displayed J2 is inferred dead: removing it gives Black66/White15+7, neutral0, matching B+44. No official dead list was provided.
Surviving upper-right11 has separate H9/J9 and J6/J7 two-point rooms.
Completed20k record: nineteen wins, eighty-seven losses, five draws; game87 unfinished and excluded. Retain20k.

## Evidence and limits

Read115/114 and consulted30 before choosing20k on a confirmed empty White board.
All31 play responses plus initial, selection and final confirmation are preserved:34 raw snapshots.
Actual-history replay legally reproduced all63 moves and matched all34 boards, physical capture counts, next move numbers and ko markers.
The SGF includes both final passes. No refused move, resignation, transport failure or missing response.
Code only inspected current/historical positions, counted groups/liberties/regions, kept records and replayed actual moves.
No engine, Monte Carlo, future-sequence search, automated move choice/ranking/recommendation or delegation.
All choices and hypothetical reading were manual; no earlier winning alternative or optimal opening is proved.
Game52's unresolved scoring discrepancy remains separate.

## Exact moves

1 B E5, 2 W C3, 3 B E2, 4 W G7, 5 B E7, 6 W C5, 7 B C6, 8 W G5, 9 B D3, 10 W C4, 11 B C2, 12 W B2, 13 B C1, 14 W B3, 15 B F3, 16 W G3, 17 B G2, 18 W H2, 19 B G4, 20 W H3, 21 B F5, 22 W H5, 23 B H4, 24 W J4, 25 B F4, 26 W J5, 27 B G6, 28 W H6, 29 B F6, 30 W H7, 31 B F7, 32 W G8, 33 B H1, 34 W J2, 35 B F8, 36 W G9, 37 B F9, 38 W B5, 39 B B6, 40 W D5, 41 B D6, 42 W D4, 43 B E4, 44 W A5, 45 B B1, 46 W A3, 47 B A6, 48 W A1, 49 B A2, 50 W J1, 51 B G1, 52 W A1, 53 B J3, 54 W J2, 55 B H3, 56 W B4, 57 B A2, 58 W H8, 59 B A4, 60 W J8, 61 B D8, 62 W pass, 63 B pass.

## Development and an outline with almost no margin

Black E5/E2/E7 occupied the center.
White C3/G7/C5/G5 tried to develop two side bases, but Black C6 at7 stopped the broad upper-left plan.
The live conditional reference before8 was ABC rows1–5 fifteen, D1–D3 three, GHJ all rows twenty-seven:45.
These were unsealed goals, not territory or proven life; D1/D2 were already ambitious beside Black E2.

C4 at10 actually joined C3/C5 after D3 contact.
Black C2/C1 undercut the lower left.
B2 at12 blocked beside C2 but started separate; B3 at14 actually joined it to C3/main.
The live outline dropped D1/D2/D3 and C1/C2, leaving left13+right27=40.
The left endpoint B1 was still open, and no completed second room existed.

G3 at16 established lower-right contact beside F3.
Black G2 undercut; H2 started separate with H1/H3/J2.
Black G4 put G3 in atari at H3; H3 at20 joined it to H2.
H5 at22 joined G5, but Black H4 immediately occupied the intended H4 bridge.
J4 at24 ataried Black G4/H4 at F4; Black F4 joined its attackers to the center.
J5 at26 joined J4/H5/G5.
H6/H7 at28/30 actually joined the upper-right branch to G7; G8/G9 retained its upper endpoint.

The losses G2/G4/H4/G6 removed four right targets.
Black H1 at33 entered the lower endpoint; G1 later joined it to G2, removing two more.
The original lower-left13 plus right21 reference was now34, below White's winning requirement38 when all81 points are assigned.
Correction to a LIVE note at28: White needs38 for a win,37 for a draw (Black44/White37+7). The earlier phrase “winning threshold37” was wrong.
D5/D4 at40/42 gained two reachable outside points, but did not make life or fix the endpoint.

## Main tactical failure: a previously suicidal cut became a legal capture

J2 at34 actually joined H2; the lower-right G3/H2/H3/J2 four had J1/J3.
At that moment Black J3 was suicide: H3/J2/J4 were White, and the lower chain still retained J1.
G9 and other work followed while J3 remained open.

At50 White J1 joined J2 and put Black H1 in atari at G1, serving as a real ko threat.
Black51 G1 answered by joining H1/G2.
Now White lower-five G3/H2/H3/J1/J2 had ONLY J3.
This changed the legality of Black J3: it would capture all five and reopen their intersections.

I reused the earlier “J3 is suicide” conclusion instead of counting after J1/G1.
White52 A1 recaptured the left ko while leaving the lower group in atari.
Black53 J3 legally captured all five.
This was a concrete avoidable reading error: count liberties after your OWN move and the reply, especially after filling one of a chain's final two liberties.
A connection point protected by suicide remains protected only while the exact liberty condition holds.
White52 J3 would actually join lower and upper right in that current position; this local legal fact does not prove a winning game or exhaustive best defense.
It would also forgo the immediate left ko recapture.

White54 J2 ataried isolated Black J3 at H3, but Black55 H3 actually joined it to H4/main.
Replacement J2 then had only H2/J1, both bordering live opponents.
Either White fill permits Black to capture the pair at the other; no two-eye life or seki.
The live “ko threat” label at54 was imprecise: White was then already holding A1, and J2 was an unsuccessful attempt to capture/recover the right.
No further stones were committed to this failed room.

## Left endpoint failure and ko-dependent life

B5 at38 joined C5; Black B6 closed the hoped-for upward extension.
D5/D4 expanded while joined, but Black D6/E4 capped both.
A5 at44 joined B5 and closed the upper edge; Black45 B1 undercut the still-open lower endpoint.
This removed the planned clean A1/A2/B1 lower room.
The problem was already present before44: the group had no completed independent-eye proof, and endpoint timing needed to be considered together with containment.
No claim that merely swapping A5 for B1 at44 guarantees life.

A3 at46 joined B3 and divided upper A4/B4 from lower A1/A2.
The lower room touched enemy B1, so it was not an unconditional eye space.
White48 A1 started isolated with sole A2.
Black49 A2 captured A1 and marked A1 ko.
White50 J1/Black51 G1 was a legal intervening exchange.
White52 A1 recaptured A2; replay verifies transient A2 ko before Black's capturing J3 reply cleared the marker.

B4 at56 joined B3/B5/C4 and made true A4.
The other claimed eye A2 still depended on isolated A1 and the ko.
Black57 A2 recaptured A1, marked A1 ko, and left the left11 sole A4.
Immediate A1 was ko-forbidden; A4 filled White's last liberty and captured no enemy, so it could not rescue the group.
White58 H8 continued on the right.
Black59 A4 physically captured A3/A5/B2/B3/B4/B5/C3/C4/C5/D4/D5 eleven.
The removal reopened many liberties for neighboring Black groups; A2 and A4 are not still isolated single-liberty stones afterward.

Physical capture ledger:
Black49 A2 captured A1;
White52 A1 captured A2;
Black53 J3 captured G3/H2/H3/J1/J2 five;
Black57 A2 captured A1;
Black59 A4 captured left11.
Black1+5+1+11=18; White1.

## Surviving right, final score and exact ledger

H8 at58 joined G8/H7.
J8 at60 joined H8 and divided the surviving upper-right into independent H9/J9 and J6/J7 two-point spaces.
All eleven upper-right stones are one living group.
Black D8 at61 occupied the empty upper left.
White62/Black63 passed.

Displayed inventory: Black30 stones+33 exclusive empties=63, White12+4=16, mixed neutral H2/J1 two.
J2 remained displayed but has no independent eyes and no external connection.
Inferred removal of J2 changes lower H2/J1/J2 into three Black-exclusive empties:
Black30+36=66; White11+4=15; neutral0.
66−(15+7)=44 matches official B+44 and final board().
The official response did not provide a dead-stone list; distinguish this inference from a supplied scoring breakdown.

Exact retrospective original45 ledger:
all left18 lost;
right lower GHJ rows1–3 nine lost;
G4/H4/G6 three lost;
45−18−9−3=15.
Equivalently GHJ rows4–9 eighteen minus G4/H4/G6 three=15.
D4/D5 were real live outside gains, but both were physically captured, so final outside gains0.
No double subtraction of G2/G1/H1: these belong to the lost lower nine.
J1 was an original target and a ko threat, not an outside gain.

## Carry forward

Retain20k. Read116/115; consult114/30 for reachable broad rooms and54/86/102 for occupied dividers.
Recompute the threatened chain after EVERY own move and opponent reply.
J1 consumed one of two liberties; G1 removed the capture option; J3 became legal by capturing the whole chain.
Complete a protected actual join before tenuki, especially when using a connection point's apparent suicide as protection.
Audit first-line endpoints early: C1 was followed by repeated other work while B1 remained open.
Do not turn an opponent-bordered lower room into a “second eye” through a vulnerable isolated ko stone.
A true A4 plus A2 ko was not unconditional life.
Keep exact White thresholds:38 wins,37 draws when all81 points are assigned.
Keep raw responses and actual-history checks; state corrections and uncertainty directly.

## Lessons to use immediately
1. Count prospective area early, especially after about 10-16 moves. With all 81 points assigned, Black needs at least 45 for a win with 7 komi; 44-37 is a draw. If there is neutral area, compare actual totals instead.
2. Center influence must yield territory, an attack, or access to a viable invasion. Game 1 built a narrow central chain while White took both sides.
3. Check two eyes for every major group before treating it as safe. Connected stones and many present liberties are not proof of life. Preserve eye space and a base before filling internal points.
4. In capture reading, rebuild the position after each capture. Captured stones open liberties for adjacent enemy groups. The D8/E9 sacrifice in game 1 overlooked this.
5. Ko eyes are not unconditional eyes. Game 1's lower D2 and upper E8 spaces depended on vulnerable isolated Black stones. Owning two such ko positions does not by itself guarantee double-ko life.
6. Do not repeat the complete opening E5 C5 E3 D7 F7 G5 G6 H6 G7 G3 without reconsidering its territorial consequences. E5 itself was not shown to be wrong.
